props.title: The Last Hurrah
props.initialSlug: Aging mayor's final political battle for legacy

sections.content: **The Last Hurrah (1958)** (1958) stands as John Ford's piercing examination of old-school American politics, featuring John Wayne in a masterful portrayal of Frank Skeffington, a veteran Irish-American mayor facing his final campaign. The film captures the death of machine politics and ward-based campaigning just as television began reshaping political landscapes. Ford's direction brings the same careful attention to urban political dynamics that he famously brought to Westerns like **The Searchers** (1956) and **Stagecoach** (1939), making this one of cinema's most insightful looks at American democracy in transition.

sections.content: The film's examination of old versus new campaign styles presaged later political classics like **The Candidate** (1972) and **Primary Colors** (1998). Ford's characteristic deep focus photography and careful composition turns smoke-filled rooms and campaign rallies into tableaus as dramatic as any Western showdown. Spencer Tracy's performance as Skeffington captures both the charm and menace of the dying breed of glad-handing political bosses.

Beyond its political commentary, **The Last Hurrah** offers a profound meditation on generational change and obsolescence - themes Ford would revisit in **The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance** (1962). The film's depiction of Irish-American political machines and ethnic voting blocs provides crucial context for understanding later films about urban politics like **State of the Union** (1948) and **Citizen Kane** (1941). sections.content: Ford's approach to political storytelling influenced decades of films about American democracy, from **Medium Cool** (1969) to **Milk** (2008). While later films would focus more on media manipulation and campaign strategy, **The Last Hurrah** remains unique in its intimate portrayal of retail politics and neighborhood-level campaigning. The film's elegiac tone for a passing political era mirrors Ford's similar treatment of the closing frontier in his Westerns.
